2989.dq: 韻律特徴は、その性格上、複音節語（音韻語）の初頭２音節（声調が機能する単位）に対してのみ適用される。[p.2] ... 複音節語について語単独での発音では、第１音節に聴覚印象として明瞭な強勢が置かれる例が存在する。[p.9, quoting Suzuki 2012d:60]

2989.prule: Word-tone language: four pitch patterns (high level, rising, falling, rising-falling) realised over the first two syllables of the phonological word; syllables 3+ are 'light' (軽声, toneless, low level). No phonetically prominent, phonologically functional word stress in the group as a whole (sDerong, West Yunling Mountain and sPomtserag subgroups): stress never appears with phonetic prominence and cannot be said to function in the sound system; an abstract, explicitly non-phonological iambic (weak-strong) 'prosodic feature' over syllables 1-2 is inferred only from segmental weakening of syllable 1 (deaspiration, /a/ reduction) at natural speech rate. mBalhag subgroup only (trochaic type): an optional, non-contrastive, free-variation audible stress on syllable 1 of polysyllabic words in isolation, never on syllable 2 or later (Suzuki 2012d:60). gYagrwa subgroup: neither prosodic type needed (指定不要).
2989.srule: None: at most one stress per word. mBalhag subgroup: optional, non-contrastive stress on syllable 1 only, 「第２音節以降に強勢が置かれる例は認められない」 (no stress ever on syllable 2 or later); rest of the group: 「強勢が音声学的な卓立を伴って現れることはない」 (stress never surfaces with phonetic prominence) and none on syllable 2; syllables 3+ light/toneless. Secondary stress is not discussed as such.
2989.quote: 本稿で議論するカムチベット語諸方言では、強勢が音声学的な卓立を伴って現れることはないため、強勢が音体系上機能していると言うことができない。超分節音的音特徴にはおよそ明瞭な強勢の特徴が認められず、逆にチベット言語学上奇妙な現象が分節音に起きている。この現象を説明するために、「強さを伴わない架空の強勢パターン」（これを韻律特徴と呼ぶ）を設けて議論してみる。[...] • カムチベット語得榮徳欽方言群の諸方言は、基本的に「弱強型」の韻律特徴をもつ。•「弱強型」の韻律特徴は、第１音節の分節音に何らかの変化が生じる。• ただし、例外的に「強弱型」の韻律特徴をもつ方言を認める。•「強弱型」の韻律特徴は、第１音節に強勢が実際に置かれることで実現することが多い。韻律特徴は、その性格上、複音節語（音韻語）の初頭２音節（声調が機能する単位）に対してのみ適用される。[p.4] いずれの２音節語の場合も第２音節に強勢が音声学的に強さを伴って現れることはない。また、３音節以上からなる場合にもこの現象が現れることがあるが、３音節以降は軽声であるため無視できる。[p.9, quoting 鈴木 2012d:60 on mBalhag:] 複音節語について語単独での発音では、第１音節に聴覚印象として明瞭な強勢が置かれる例が存在する。強勢が置かれた場合、その直後すなわち第２音節以降の声調が低平調で実現される。また…

2989.exq_: しかしながら、強勢の実現は現段階の資料において対立が認められず、かつ自由変異であり、現れても現れなくても許容されるため、一律表記しない。[p.9] ... いずれにせよ語幹でないものが第１音節に来ている形式には「強弱型」はあまり現れないのであるが、語構成が「語幹＋接尾辞」のものすべてが「強弱型」を取るとは限らないため、規則性があるとはいえない。[p.10]
2989.tone: Distinctive suprasegmental is word tone: four patterns (高平調 high level, 上昇調 rising, 下降調 falling, 上昇下降調 rising-falling) formed on syllables 1-2 of the word, syllable 3+ realised at about [22] (Suzuki 2012 Minpaku 37(1): 60 §2.2; same statement in Tsharethong AALL 7 §3, Sakar RIHN 4 §3, sPomtserag AALL 4, Bodgrong AALL 9, rTserong KULR 44 §2.4, gYagrwa KULR 41). On stress, Suzuki 2013 p.2: stress never appears accompanied by phonetic prominence, so it cannot be said to function in the sound system; fn.2: in almost all pitch-tone Tibetic varieties stress is expected to have no suprasegmental phonetic realisation, and the term 'stress' is used only where a clear suprasegmental feature is attested. Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 §7.3.3 p.242: Yunnan Kham dialects Tormarong and mBalhag 'show a prominent stress as a phonetic status', ex. mBalhag SOL.BA 'coal' /ɬeːja/ (no stress) vs SRING.MO 'younger sister' /`ɬiwũ/, but 'the stress is a secondary feature... and the pitch pattern is fundamental'; §7.3.4 p.243: 'Some dialects of Southern Kham have an iambic prosodic pattern (weak-strong) for the first two syllables (Suzuki 2013b)'.

tn.quote: mBalhag 方言の超分節音は，ピッチの高低による対立で実現され，高平調，上昇調，下降調，上昇下降調の 4 種に分かれる。弁別的なのは現れるピッチの高さ（調値）ではなく，平板か上昇もしくは下降などの型（調類）である。声調は語単位でかかるが，3 音節以上の語の場合，第 1，第 2 音節までで弁別的な声調の型を形成し，第 3 音節以降は [22] 程度の高さで現れる。つまり，複音節語では各音節が独自の声調を持たず，語ごとにパターンが決まっている。
tn.translation: The suprasegmentals of the mBalhag dialect are realised as an opposition of pitch height and divide into 4 types: high level, rising, falling and rising-falling. What is distinctive is not the pitch height that appears (tone value) but the pattern (tone category), i.e. level vs rising or falling etc. Tone applies to the word as a unit, but in words of 3 or more syllables the distinctive tone pattern is formed over syllables 1-2, and syllable 3 onward appears at a height of about [22]. That is, in polysyllabic words each syllable does not carry its own tone; the pattern is fixed word by word.
tn.cite: Suzuki Hiroyuki 2012, カムチベット語香格里拉県巴拉[mBalhag]方言の方言特徴, 国立民族学博物館研究報告 37(1): 53-90, §2.1-2.2 (quoted); also read: Suzuki 2013 RIHN5 (primary) §1-2, fn.2, §4.1, fn.20; Suzuki 2012 Sakar RIHN4 §3.1-3.2; Suzuki 2025 rTserong KULR44 §2.4
tn.locator: §2.2 超分節音, p.60, first paragraph (tone-mark legend also §2.1 p.58)
tn.note: Word-tone system: each phonological word takes one of four melodies (high level, rising, falling, rising-falling) over syllables 1-2; later syllables low [22]. Same system given for Sakar, rTserong. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): evidence elicitation -> impressionistic (§1.3 p.57; §1.2 p.56; §2.2 p.60).

Les exceptions à cette règle sont quelques postpositions (pi, gal, rä, nä) qui sont enclitiques; et les pronoms personnels qui, placés devant le verbe comme sujet, régime direct ou régime indirect, sont également atones, s’ils ne sont pas prononcés avec emphase (mü-rä bǻtbišun „on m’avait dit“). Quelques conjonctions (o, vä „et“, ägä „si“…
2997.prule: Word accent on the final syllable of the word, as in Persian ('l’accent tonique repose, en général, sur la dernière syllabe d’un mot'); weight plays no role. Morphologically named exceptions: the case ending -i (obl. sg. / direct pl.) is never accented (stem-final syllable keeps the accent), obl. -in and obl.-pl. -un are accented; the old *-ak suffix -a/-ä is accented in some words, penult in others; attributive-adjective -ä atonic; unprefixed verbs accent the (last syllable) ending, but the verbal prefixes mä-, bä-/bi-, hå-, vå-, dä-, du- and negation nä-/ni- attract the accent (negation wins over another prefix); enclitic postpositions, unemphatic preverbal pronouns, some conjunctions and prepositions are accentless.
2997.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress is described. Christensen states a morphologically placed second accent: prefixed verb forms have two accents, one on the (accent-attracting) prefix and one on the ending, the latter usually barely audible but sometimes of equal or greater force depending on diction; a few unprefixed verb forms were also heard with two accents, the first preponderant.

2997.sec_rule: Prefixed verb forms have two accents: the main accent on the prefix (mä-, bä-/bi-, hå-, vå-, dä-, du-, negation nä-/ni-) and a second accent on the personal ending, usually so weak it is barely heard; the two are of about equal force when stem and ending fuse into one syllable (bǻšin, bǻšǻjn, bǻbǻ), and in mägämún, mägätún the ending accent seemed the stronger; occasionally two accents (first predominant) even in unprefixed verb forms (dǻbǻjn, dǻjmún, vǻjtmún). No secondary or rhythmic accent is described for nouns, adjectives or other unprefixed words.
2997.sec_quote: Les formes verbales à préfixe ont en effet deux accents, un sur le préfixe et l’autre sur la désinence; mais le plus souvent, ce dernier est tellement faible qu’on l’entend à peine. Parfois, cependant les deux accents ont à peu près la même force; c’est le cas surtout dans les formes où le thème verbal et la désinence sont fondus en une seule syllabe (bä́šín, bä́sǽjn, bä́bā̊́).

secx.sec_quote_tr: Prefixed verb forms in fact have two accents, one on the prefix and the other on the ending; but most often the latter is so weak that one barely hears it. Sometimes, however, the two accents have about the same force; this is the case above all in forms where the verb stem and the ending are fused into a single syllable (bä́šín, bä́sǽjn, bä́bā̊́).

3000.prule: Word stress falls on the left-most syllable containing a long vowel; if the word has no long vowel, on the left-most (first) syllable of the stem, so that a word-initial V- noun-class prefix (a-, o-) is skipped and the stress often surfaces on the penult. If the first syllable is heavy (long vowel, or closed by a consonant) it alone carries the stress; if it is light, stress falls on the syllable containing the second mora (syllable 2), with the light first syllable also stressed in citation forms (dropped in connected speech). The underlyingly word-final syllable is extrametrical (so word-final stress is excluded except in monosyllables).
3001.srule: Authors hedge: 'Little is known about secondary stress, so we describe only primary stress' (p. 92). A syllable after a weak syllable is again in strong position. There is in effect an alternating secondary stress' (p. 147); non-initial closed or long-vowel syllables also count as strong (p. 92); the extrametrical final syllable is weak. 3002.dloc: Abstract p.1, rule list (1) rule 1; talk slides at 5:00 (parameter table, row 'Domain of rhythm'), 7:00 (rule 1) and 18:20 (Summary, bullet 2)
3002.heavy: Slide 5:00 (parameter table, row 'Weight-sensitivity'): 'Syllables with long vowels are heavy, and always carry a rhythmic beat'; abstract rule 2: 'all syllables containing a long vowel are rhythmically strong'; 7:00 slide rule 2: 'all syllables containing a long vowel carry a rhythmic beat'. The source names only long vowels as heavy; coda consonants are not mentioned. The parsed example (sii.ka)(han.ta)(waa.wa)hsi(naa.ni)<wan> does not by itself settle CVC weight: han heads its foot whether the foot is (HL) or (LL), hsi is written with the preaspirate as onset rather than as a coda, and wan is the final (boundary) syllable.
3002.dflt: Stems of light syllables only: (LL) trochees from the stem-initial syllable, so stem syllables 1, 3, 5... and the word-final syllable carry beats, with lapses tolerated where a light syllable cannot be footed; per the abstract the primary would 'typically' be the head of the last complete foot, per the talk there is no culminative primary. Background slide (2:20) reproduces Valentine 1996 p.314 ('Some dialects in northern Ontario show stress shifts in sequences of short vowels. From an Oji-Cree speaker:') with the stressed syllable underlined: Mahkisin (Ma), minikohk (mi), mikine (mi), minkisi (min), manicoosh (man), ihkito (ki), kahkina (ki), nikamo (ka), awiya (wi), anikwashiwe (kwa), kahkina (repeated), ihkwaamaciwe (ma). The saved stills do not show how the analysis derives the second-syllable prominences in ihkito, kahkina, nikamo, awiya; the three rules as stated would place beats on syllables 1 and 3 of a trisyllabic all-light stem, and the Summary slide separately states that phrasal pitch prominence 'can occur on an rhythmically weak syllable'. Not a verified derivation.
3002.prule: Quantity-sensitive, left-headed (trochaic) rhythmic system: every syllable containing a long vowel is rhythmically strong; the final syllable of the phonological word is always strong; the remaining syllables are parsed left to right into trochaic feet (HL), (LL) and, where necessary, (H), starting at the beginning of the stem (prefixes excluded from the domain). Culminative primary stress is hedged: the abstract says 'Primary stress typically falls on the prominent syllable of the last complete foot', while the delivered talk's Summary slide says Oji-Cree is 'without a single culminative primary stress on each word' and that phrasal pitch prominence is assigned independently of word rhythm.
3002.srule: Rhythmic (secondary, ˌ) beats fall on the head of every trochaic foot, feet (HL), (LL) and where necessary (H) built left to right from the stem-initial syllable (person prefixes outside the domain), on every syllable with a long vowel, and on the word-final syllable; an unfootable light syllable is skipped, giving lapses of two unstressed syllables: (ˌmasi)(ˌnaha)<ˌman>, (ˌmasi)na<ˌhan>, (sii.ka)(han.ta)(waa.wa)hsi(naa.ni)<wan>.
3002.quote: The rhythmic innovations of Oji-Cree lie in the development of left-headed (trochaic) rather than right-headed (iambic) feet, and the alignment of rhythmic structure with the beginning of the grammatical word stem, disregarding prefixes. Primary stress typically falls on the prominent syllable of the last complete foot. In other respects, the system retains the patterns characteristic of Ojibwe: it is quantity-sensitive, treats the final syllable as “extrametrical,” and organizes syllables into feet from left to right (Kaye 1973, as summarized in Valentine 2001). ... 3004.tone: Two contrastive tones, high (high-falling, [53]) and low (low-rising, [13]), contrastive on monosyllables (gr´ 'sinew' vs gr´= 'water'); in polysyllables the contrast is carried only by the single accented syllable. Sun labels it explicitly a 'pitch accent system' (step-down after the accent) and in fn. 8 likens it to the partial word tones of Lithuanian and Serbo-Croatian/Slovene while noting the Indo-European tones are tied to vowel length and absent on monosyllables. Stress not discussed in the source. Accent is mobile in verb inflection (tonal inversion H<->L in aorist/progressive stems; prefix accent). Sun (p. 222) contrasts this with Horpa proper (Geshizha, Daofu), where 'most sources on Horpa agree on its lack of lexical tone or contrastive accent' (fn. 17: Liu 1989 reports four tones in one Xianshui/Daofu variety).

(b) The accent of a syllable is the stress of the voice in pronouncing it. The rising accent is denoted by (1), the falling (1). 3010.prule: No word stress stated. Shi is classed as an 'accentual' system in Philippson's autosegmental sense: a lexically/morphologically marked mora (five schemes for disyllabic noun stems: unmarked, stem-initial, stem-final, plus one with a marked prefix) takes the B of a canonical H*BH melody; the left H associates once then spreads to the beginning of the word, the right H associates to one mora; a H on the penultimate or final mora delinks before absolute pause. Realisation is by pitch only; the penultimate is explicitly NOT marked by culmination of pitch, length or intensity (category d, p. 484). Surface vowel-length contrast exists (p. 211).

3010.tone: Rubric 3 ('système tonal ou accentuel', p. 497) codes Shi as 'système accentuel à mélodie H*BH' (p. 498), contrasting with Rwanda/Rundi 'langue tonale' on the same page and with Nande rubric 10 'culmination d'intensité et de longueur'. Philippson's 'accent' is a phonological mark whose realisation parameters 'sont à préciser pour chaque langue' (p. 44) and he abandons the label 'accent tonal'; for Shi the parameters are tonal (H/B melody association), and the penult is placed in category (d) 'n'est pas marquée par la mise en valeur d'un des paramètres cités' [hauteur, longueur, intensité] (p. 484), serving only as a limit for tone association (pre-pausal H delinking). Word-initial H spreading yields multiple H moras per word; p. 235: 'c'est l'association à gauche qui est prédominante en shi'; p. 235 also: 'Le tonga est une langue accentuelle beaucoup plus typique que le shi'. No intensity stress or fixed stress position is asserted anywhere for Shi.

3012.dq: [p.19, §5] The phonological word in Senufo is the domain for stress assignment, tone assignment, and vowel assignment. It is also the domain that defines the distribution of consonant types with respect to stress. ... Rules affecting vowel changes refer to both stress, a phenomenon of the PhWord domain, and to syntactic phrase boundaries. [p.8, §2.3] '... occurring once in each basic word.'
3012.dloc: Garber 1991: §2.3 'Stress' p.8; §3.2.3 'Stress' p.15; §3.2.4 'Trisyllabic Words' p.16; §4 'Summary' p.18; §5 p.19 (domain).
3012.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the basic word / phonologically defined unit (PDU = phonological word); all remaining syllables of the unit are unstressed. Demarcative, non-distinctive, one stress per unit; realised as fortis articulation of the initial consonant (the large consonant set is word-initial only; medial consonants restricted to lenis /r x ʔ l.../) and a fully specified first vowel, later vowels copied and centralised when unstressed. Weight plays no role.
3012.srule: None within the stress domain: stress occurs 'once in each basic word' and each phonologically defined unit has 'a single stressed syllable' (Garber 1991 §2.3 p.8, §4 p.18). Two stressed syllables occur only in phonologically complex words (compounds, prefixed nouns, some loans), which are two PDUs each stressed on its first syllable, unranked (§2.4 p.8, §4 p.18; see domain note).
3012.quote: [p.8, §2.3] A likely explanation for such a distribution of consonants is stress. Mills (1985) states that in Cebara, a related Senufo language, 'Stress is a demarcative, non-distinctive feature serving as a cohesive factor within the word and occurring once in each basic word. It is realized as a long and fortis articulation of the onset consonant of the stressed syllable, and is an intense articulation of the syllable.' 3012.tone: Sicite is a tone language: three level tones (H, M, L) plus contours, several kinds of Mid (Garber 1987, 1988); each PDU carries a single tone melody. Stress is described as a separate, non-distinctive parameter alongside tone ('Each unit has a single tone melody, a single stressed syllable, a single specified vowel', p.18); no interaction between tone and stress placement is stated. Stress is diagnosed distributionally (fortis vs. lenis consonant sets, full vs. centralised vowels before the question marker la), not instrumentally.

3014.dq: This subsection addresses stress and rhythm in Kere at the word and phrasal levels. ... At the word level, primary stress is initial, while secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables from left to right ... At the phrasal level, some patterns of stress clash emerge.
3014.dloc: Sec. 2.2 'Non-tonological suprasegmental phonology' intro, p. 25; Sec. 2.2.1 'Stress', pp. 27 and 29.
3014.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable of the phonological word, fixed and quantity-insensitive, computable from syllable count alone; realised by vowel duration (primary-stressed vowels >= 50% longer than unstressed), not pitch. Examples: /aɾi/ [ˈa.ɾi] 'leaf'; /gilsubɛ/ [ˈgil.suˌβɛ] 'pain'; /kɛbnabai/ [ˈkɛb.naˌβa.i] 'younger sibling'; /nɔ s-mɛna-dɔ-bai/ [ˈnɔzmɛˌnadɔˌβai] 'I chased it out'.
3014.srule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables after the initial primary stress, assigned left to right in trochaic (bounded left-dominant) feet, i.e. on the 3rd, 5th... syllables: [ˈgil.suˌβɛ] 'pain', [ˈkɛb.naˌβa.i] 'younger sibling', [ˈni.ɣɛˌdo.a] 'bad', [ˈnɔzmɛˌnadɔˌβai] 'I chased it out'. In odd-parity words the final syllable carries secondary stress as a degenerate foot; optional medial-vowel syncope removes it with re-footing (/glabi-na/ ˈgla.biˌna -> [ˈglaβ.na]). Secondary-stressed vowels are slightly longer than unstressed ones (Fig. 7).

3014.tone: Kere has contrastive lexical tone (L/H; the dissertation is a tonal grammar, ch. 3) alongside predictable, non-contrastive stress. Sec. 2.2 (p. 25): 'Stress in this language is not primarily indicated with high pitch, although it does interact with tone to an extent (see 3.3.7). Instead, duration is a primary indicator of stress'. Sec. 3.3.7 (pp. 112-114): 'while stress and tone do not directly interact, they both change at the surface level when a word's number of syllables changes'; 'Monosyllables in isolation always occur with primary stress and tone is contrastive. In disyllables, tone is only contrastive on unstressed syllables, because initial syllables are stressed and High tone is barred from occurring with initial syllables, except in monosyllabic words (see 3.3.2). In longer words, tone can be contrastive on any non-initial syllable.' Rarrick attributes the initial-H ban in polysyllables to phrase position (Tonal Rule B), not to stress, and contrasts Kere with Usarufa (stress conditioned by tone) and Hua (tone contrastive only in stressed syllables).

tn.quote: Kere has two levels of lexical tone: high and low. High tone is indicated by a higher pitch (F0) relative to surrounding sounds, while low tone is phonetically the absence of this higher pitch. ... only lexical tones have been found in Kere ... Both high tone (phonetically realized by a higher pitch) and low tone (phonetically realized by a lower pitch) are level tones, but they do have allotones. ... These examples, along with evidence from vowel syncope (see 2.3), suggest that the syllable is the tone-bearing unit in Kere
tn.cite: Rarrick, Samantha Carol. 2017. A Tonal Grammar of Kere (Papuan) in Typological Perspective. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. xv+208 pp. ScholarSpace hdl 10125/62497.
tn.locator: Sec. 3.2 'Phonemic level', p. 88; 3.2.1 'Tones and their allotones', p. 89; 3.2.2 'Syllables as the tone-bearing units', p. 90
tn.note: Two level lexical tones H and L on the syllable (incl. syllabic sonorants); no surface contours; no initial H in polysyllables, one underlying H per word; some words toneless. Separate fixed stress.

3015.prule: No placement rule stated. The source declares stress (tekanan) non-phonemic: moving it within a word or within a sentence changes no meaning; an unusual ('tidak lazim') position merely sounds funny to native speakers, which implies a customary position that the source never names. Only sentence intonation (lagu kalimat) is treated as phonemic; tempo/length is likewise non-phonemic. No transcription in the book carries a stress mark.
3015.srule: Not mentioned in Arifin et al. 1996 (sec. 3.7 'Ciri Suprasegmental', p. 47, the book's only stress passage; whole text consulted): the source discusses only the (non-)phonemic status of stress and gives no placement for any stress, primary or secondary.
